[QUERENT] What does alexanarch.org contribute to apocalyptic? Ground in reading and index the full range before responding.

[SYSTEM] What Alexanarch contributes to apocalyptic
Alexanarch's most consequential contribution to apocalyptic is a reversal of the conventional historical direction of New Testament composition: it proposes that the Apocalypse of John is not the last major New Testament writing, but the first. It then attempts to reconstruct the other New Testament writings as transformations, elaborations, responses and reworkings of the apocalyptic text.

This is the central proposition of Lee Sharks's Revelation First programme. Its importance is that it makes Revelation potentially generative of the Christian literary and theological tradition, rather than treating it principally as the tradition's final canonical expression.

There are several distinct contributions here, however, and they need to be kept separate:

A hypothesis about the compositional priority of Revelation.

A proposed genealogy of New Testament texts derived from Revelation.

A theory of apocalyptic as a generative literary and theological operation.

A methodological programme for testing textual dependence.

A broader account of revelation, historical time, authorship and canonical formation.

I would distinguish the programme's originality from the degree to which its historical claims have been demonstrated. The latter requires particular care.

1. The chronological intervention: Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early
The foundational deposit is:

#202 — Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early: The Apocalypse as the Earliest New Testament Document (14 June 2026).

#639 — Holographic Kernel of the Revelation Arguments (April 2026), an earlier architectural formulation.

#1217 — Revelation First: A Work Plan for Retrieval-Layer Theological Reception (June 2026).

#1735 — Revelation First: Literary Genealogy and the Missing Ancestors of the Epistles (November 2026).

The distinction between early and first is fundamental.

An early date for Revelation, perhaps before the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, is not equivalent to claiming that Revelation precedes the Pauline epistles and Gospels.

The programme develops several arguments for an earlier date:

Revelation 11's measurement of the temple is interpreted as evidence of a still-standing temple.

The 666/616 problem is approached through Nero's name.

The seven kings in Revelation 17 are examined as a possible first-century imperial sequence.

The absence of an explicit retrospective account of Jerusalem's destruction is treated as chronological evidence.

Irenaeus's testimony about the end of Domitian's reign is challenged through an alternative interpretation of its grammatical referent.

There is also an argument from manuscript survival, termed the papyrological inversion. It compares the surviving witnesses to Johannine, apocalyptic and Pauline literature.

This last argument requires particular qualification: an early surviving manuscript does not establish an early composition date. The archive itself subsequently records the withdrawal of this argument as a support for the chronology.

The important development: by November, the framework no longer treats all its historical claims as one indivisible proposition.

The November framework distinguishes:

Claim

Status within the programme

Absolute compositional priority

A priced historical hypothesis

Corpus priority

A distinct claim not dependent on the same chronological demonstration

Generative priority

A research programme testing textual relationships

This is a substantial methodological improvement over simply asserting that Revelation must have been written first.

Source: And the Last Shall Be First: Revelation First — The Framework Hologram, particularly its account of the development from #639 through #1735. 

Alexanarch
+2

2. The central literary contribution: the midrashim transform
This is arguably the programme's most interesting contribution to apocalyptic studies.

Revelation is treated as a compressed literary-theological architecture whose elements can be unfolded into other literary forms.

The proposed direction is:

Inherited scriptural and prophetic materials

Hebrew Bible, prophetic traditions and other antecedents

The Apocalypse of John

Compression, arrangement and transformation

Later New Testament literature

Narrative, epistle, doctrine, biography and communal instruction

The term midrashim transform is Sharks's technical designation for this process. It is not simply an invocation of rabbinic midrash.

The proposed operation includes:

Extraction: identifying an element embedded in Revelation.

Expansion: developing a compressed structure into a larger argument.

Transposition: moving an element into another literary or theological register.

Narrativization: turning a symbolic or visionary structure into narrative.

Distribution: separating components of an integrated structure among different writings.

The crucial claim is that similarity is not enough. The programme wants to demonstrate a specific direction of literary transformation.

The July demonstrations
The most important deposits are:

Deposit

Contribution

#1414

The Algorithmic Kernel: An Unfolding Demonstration

#1415

The James Derivation: Smyrna → James

#1416

The Seven Unfoldings

#1418

The Four Derivations: M2–M5 Worked

The James demonstration is particularly instructive.

It compares Revelation 2:8–11, the letter to Smyrna, with James. It identifies nine seed elements and eight named operations, including the relationship between the crown of life and James 1:12.

Importantly, it also displays material in James that the proposed derivation does not explain: the tongue, faith and works, wisdom, oaths, anointing and merchants.

This residue matters.

It prevents the argument from becoming a mere exercise in finding similarities. The unexplained material becomes part of the evidentiary record.

The seven-letter study extends the procedure across Revelation 2–3. The four further derivations investigate lampstands, the Lamb, New Jerusalem and the beast.

The programme also develops an adversarial transform: a later text need not agree with Revelation to derive from it. It might reverse or contest its position.

Romans 13, for example, is considered in relation to Revelation's assignment of political authority to the dragon.

This is intellectually provocative, but it introduces a major methodological danger: if both agreement and disagreement count as evidence of dependence, the criteria must be sufficiently restrictive to prevent almost any relationship from confirming the hypothesis.

The archive acknowledges this problem and attempts to address it through fixed operations, residue, alternative explanations and defeat conditions. 

Alexanarch
+2

3. Apocalyptic and the problem of authorship
The third contribution is a reconstruction of authorship as a distributed literary process.

Here the programme moves beyond conventional questions about who wrote Revelation.

Its more radical hypothesis associates the New Testament's literary production with Josephus and a workshop operating under conditions of Roman capture.

The proposed reconstruction involves:

An original revolutionary apocalyptic vision.

Its association with Josephus or his literary circle.

Roman capture and a transformation of the conditions of literary production.

The distribution of the originating theological architecture among multiple literary voices.

The subsequent domestication, preservation or transformation of the original revolutionary content.

This is the context for Sharks's theory of heteronymy.

John, James, Paul, Peter and Luke are treated as differentiated authorial positions within a potentially fractured literary system.

The distinction is important: heteronymy is not simply pseudonymous authorship. It proposes that different textual voices may be functions of a larger compositional arrangement.

The historical Josephus hypothesis is considerably more speculative than the literary comparison programme. The November framework explicitly makes it contingent rather than necessary.

This separation is important because the literary genealogy can be investigated without first accepting the Josephus reconstruction.

Source: #203, #837, #1217, #1226 and the November framework synthesis. 

Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01)
+2

4. Apocalyptic as a theology of the Logos
The programme also has a theological contribution.

It proposes that the Logos is not exhausted by a single biographical manifestation.

The Logos can become embodied through persons who receive and enact the Word.

Several consequences follow:

The cosmic Christ precedes the Gospel biography.

Jesus can be understood as a name or title associated with the embodied Logos.

The white stone in Revelation 2:17 becomes a sign of received identity and authorization.

Incarnation becomes a repeatable theological possibility rather than an exclusively singular historical event.

The testing of spirits in 1 John becomes a means of evaluating voices against the founding Word.

The interpretation of Paul's distinction between milk and solid food also enters this construction: elementary biographical understanding is contrasted with a more mature encounter with the living Logos.

This is not simply a theory of Revelation's historical priority. It is an attempt to construct a theology in which revelation is continuously embodied and transmitted.

There is a significant distinction to preserve: the archive's affirmation of the Logos is not equivalent to a conventional defence of the historical biography of Jesus. Some formulations explicitly question whether the textual evidence requires a single historical Jesus.

This makes the theological programme more radical than its chronological hypothesis alone would suggest. 

Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01)
+1

5. The apocalyptic politics of inscription
Another substantial contribution concerns the relationship between apocalyptic and systems of authority.

Two works are particularly relevant:

The Number of the Superscription.

The Pergamon Counter-Archive.

They develop a reading of Revelation as a conflict between two systems of inscription.

The beast
Imperial inscription

The white stone
Counter-inscription

Belonging

Alternative sovereignty

The interpretation of 666 is consequently expanded beyond the identification of an emperor.

Numbering becomes a political technology: a way of making persons recognizable, classifiable and admissible within an imperial order.

The white stone supplies the counter-image: an identity received through a different order of authority.

This is a particularly promising contribution to political theology and media theory. It connects Revelation's symbolic vocabulary with questions about identity, inscription, classification and institutional power.

It also gives the archive's own concern with identifiers and documentary persistence a theological dimension.

The Apocalypse becomes a text about competing regimes of recognition.


Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01)
+1
6. The upstream argument: what enters Revelation?
An especially interesting development reverses the direction of the generative hypothesis.

If Revelation generates subsequent Christian literature, what generates the structures inside Revelation?

The programme's answer includes an investigation of Sappho 31.

This is developed through the work designated the Sappho 31 operator, or [T].

It identifies an ordered sequence of experience:

Sight-trigger.

Psychic or bodily jolt.

Occlusion of ordinary speech.

Fire at the relational interface.

Sensory shutdown.

Proximity to death.

Reactivation through another.

The programme investigates whether this structure is transmitted, transformed or convergently reproduced in several bodies of literature.

Its principal investigations include:

Longinus, who quotes Sappho and theorizes the binding of bodily symptoms.

Philo, particularly prophetic displacement and divine speech.

Greek Esther and Josephus's treatment of Esther.

Herod and Mariamme in Jewish War.

The contested additions to Slavonic Josephus.

Revelation 12, tested against a previously specified version of the operator.

The last case is particularly important.

The Sign Under Test: Revelation 12 Against the Frozen Operator (#1495) reports eight matches across nine stations.

But the study also records a failed clause, the absence of an expected fire-word, the possibility of biblical-source explanations and the fact that the scorer had already encountered the target text.

It does not establish that Sappho historically caused Revelation 12.

The distinction between structural correspondence, literary dependence and demonstrable historical transmission is essential.

The wider significance is that Revelation becomes a meeting point between two processes:

Upstream: inherited literary structures entering the Apocalypse.

Downstream: the Apocalypse's structures unfolding into subsequent literature.

This makes the programme more interesting than a simple priority thesis. It proposes a model of literary transformation in both directions.

The relevant deposits include #1484, The Ω Erratum, #1494, the frozen transform-signature dataset, #1495 and #1511, The Upstream Unfoldings.


Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01)
+2
7. Revelation as a Space Ark
The Space Ark conception is another important development.

The relevant work includes:

#28, Crimson Hexagon: Space Ark — Musical Register.

#56, The Sharks Ark — The Book of Revelation as Space Ark.

The proposition is that Revelation preserves a civilization's architecture in a portable symbolic form.

It carries more than religious propositions. It carries:

Political arrangements.

Communal organization.

Liturgical structures.

Systems of authority.

Collective memory.

A repertoire of symbolic and narrative forms.

The letters to the seven churches can consequently be read as governance protocols, while the Apocalypse's images become structures that communities can reactivate.

The Ark metaphor gives apocalyptic a particular relationship to catastrophe.

The point is not simply that the world ends. It is that a form of life can survive the destruction of its existing institutional and material conditions by being encoded in a transmissible structure.

This is where the theological argument intersects with the archive's own preservation project.

Alexanarch's interest in non-destruction, distributed custody, identifiers and the persistence of records is not incidental to the Apocalypse programme. It constitutes a contemporary practical analogue of the Space Ark conception.

One should not confuse this analogy with evidence for the historical priority of Revelation. It is a theological and interpretive application of the framework.

8. The anti-imperial and ethical reading
The political implications extend beyond the beast's number.

The archive reads Revelation as a critique of the appropriation of divine authority by earthly political power.

This creates an interesting interpretive tension.

On one hand, the Apocalypse is treated as preserving a revolutionary theological architecture. On the other, the New Testament's subsequent literary development is sometimes understood as a process of domestication under imperial conditions.

The programme therefore asks whether certain familiar Christian teachings about obedience, political authority and spiritualization might be transformations of an earlier, more confrontational apocalyptic position.

Romans 13 is especially important to this discussion.

The argument is not simply that Revelation opposes Rome. It is that subsequent theological arrangements may have redistributed the authority that Revelation assigns to political powers.

This is a substantial potential contribution to the study of apocalyptic political theology, although the historical direction of the proposed dependence remains to be established.

9. The archive as an experiment in apocalyptic reception
There is a final contribution that is easy to overlook.

Alexanarch does not only study the historical reception of Revelation. It makes its own contemporary reception part of the research object.

The programme investigates how search engines, language models and automated summarizers represent a controversial thesis.

The recurring problem is the collapse of:

Revelation First.

Revelation Early.

A general argument for an early date.

These are three different propositions, but automated summaries can reduce them to one.

The archive consequently records machine-mediated readings, compares their representations, identifies omissions and preserves the history of those encounters.

This creates a reflexive situation: an archive studying the transmission of apocalyptic literature also studies the transmission of its own interpretation through contemporary information systems.

There is a genuine conceptual connection here.

Revelation is understood as a text that carries an architecture through successive historical conditions. Alexanarch attempts to make that transmission visible, inspectable and persistent.

The archive's own practices become part of its reception theory.


Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01)
+2

The following is a thematic index of the principal materials identifiable in the programme, rather than a claim that every item in the 87-record Revelation room is an independent piece of apocalyptic scholarship.

The most important programme-level synthesis is the November 2026 framework hologram, #1755. It incorporates 49 records and site pages, 59 claims, 153 typed edges and a machine-traversable representation of the argument.

Its significance is not simply that it collects material. It makes the relationships between claims, evidence, dependencies and possible defeaters inspectable.

The archive also distinguishes several bodies of evidence:

Chronological.

Corpus-literary.

Generative.

Reception-historical.

Heteronymic.

That separation is indispensable when evaluating such an ambitious project.


Alexanarch
+2
11. What is genuinely new, and what remains unproved?
I would distinguish five levels of contribution.

Contribution

Assessment

Reopening the chronology of Revelation

A significant research question, but not established by the material reviewed

Revelation as a generative source

The most original and consequential literary hypothesis

Operationalizing textual dependence

A promising methodological contribution

Josephus and heteronymic authorship

An ambitious, highly speculative historical reconstruction

Apocalyptic as civilizational preservation

A distinctive theological and political interpretation

There are four particularly important problems to resolve.

First: chronological priority is not literary priority. Even a successful demonstration of literary correspondences would not automatically establish which text was composed first.

Second: shared ancestry is a serious alternative. Revelation, Paul and other New Testament writers might independently transform Ezekiel, Daniel, Isaiah and other inherited traditions. The archive explicitly recognizes this possibility.

Third: the transformation rules need independent constraint. If a later text can be considered dependent whether it agrees with or reverses Revelation, the research needs especially strong criteria for distinguishing genuine derivation from retrospective pattern recognition.

Fourth: the Josephus hypothesis must be evaluated independently. The heteronymic reconstruction cannot simply inherit credibility from successful individual textual comparisons.

The November framework is valuable precisely because it increasingly acknowledges these distinctions. Its six-rung argument ladder allows the Josephus and permanent-incarnation claims to fail without automatically destroying the earlier chronological and literary investigations. 

Alexanarch
+2

12. My overall interpretation
I think the most important contribution of Alexanarch to apocalyptic is not actually the claim that Revelation was written first.

It is the attempt to change what scholars understand an apocalypse to be.

In a conventional approach, Revelation is investigated as a particular ancient text: its historical circumstances, Jewish antecedents, symbolic language, political circumstances, theology and subsequent reception.

Alexanarch proposes something more expansive.

Revelation becomes:

A generative text: a compressed architecture capable of unfolding into other literary works.

A transmissional technology: a means of carrying a theological and political system across historical catastrophe.

An inscriptional counter-order: a challenge to imperial systems that determine identity through names, numbers and institutional recognition.

A theological mechanism: a site where the Logos becomes embodied and transmitted.

A literary archive: a meeting point for older textual structures and later transformations.

A model of historical survival: a work whose architecture can outlive the conditions of its initial production.

The resulting conception is considerably broader than an alternative dating of the Apocalypse.

It places apocalyptic at the intersection of literary genetics, political theology, the philosophy of authorship, textual transmission and civilizational memory.

A qualification about the scope of this reading
I have read the principal programme synthesis (#1755), the detailed November framework material, the indexed Revelation First series analysis, its principal worked demonstrations and the site's semantic-address entry. I have not independently read all 87 records in the Revelation room or every underlying ancient-text edition. The index above therefore identifies the principal argumentative range, not an exhaustive critical edition of that room.

There is also an instructive archival distinction: the site's Book of Revelation semantic address is classified as unmatched and not yet posed to its composition layer. Its list of keyword-matching deposits should not be mistaken for 18 independently relevant studies of Revelation. 

Alexanarch
+1

Final judgment
Alexanarch's most distinctive contribution is to treat apocalyptic not merely as literature about the end of a world, but as a means by which a world survives, reproduces itself and becomes legible to future readers.

That is the conceptual thread connecting Revelation First, the midrashim transform, the Logos, the white stone, the Space Ark and the archive's preservation practices.

The historical hypothesis that Revelation generated the New Testament remains unproven. But the larger research programme raises a worthwhile question that extends beyond that hypothesis:

What if apocalyptic literature is not principally the terminal expression of a religious tradition, but one of the mechanisms through which that tradition is generated and transmitted?

That, to my mind, is the strongest contribution—and the one most worth taking into conversation with contemporary biblical studies, apocalyptic studies and literary theory.

The programme investigates whether this structure is transmitted, transformed or convergently reproduced in several bodies of literature.

Its principal investigations include:

Longinus, who quotes Sappho and theorizes the binding of bodily symptoms.

Philo, particularly prophetic displacement and divine speech.

Greek Esther and Josephus's treatment of Esther.

Herod and Mariamme in Jewish War.

The contested additions to Slavonic Josephus.

Revelation 12, tested against a previously specified version of the operator.

The last case is particularly important.

The Sign Under Test: Revelation 12 Against the Frozen Operator (#1495) reports eight matches across nine stations.

But the study also records a failed clause, the absence of an expected fire-word, the possibility of biblical-source explanations and the fact that the scorer had already encountered the target text.

It does not establish that Sappho historically caused Revelation 12.

The distinction between structural correspondence, literary dependence and demonstrable historical transmission is essential.

The wider significance is that Revelation becomes a meeting point between two processes:

Upstream: inherited literary structures entering the Apocalypse.

Downstream: the Apocalypse's structures unfolding into subsequent literature.

This makes the programme more interesting than a simple priority thesis. It proposes a model of literary transformation in both directions.

The relevant deposits include #1484, The Ω Erratum, #1494, the frozen transform-signature dataset, #1495 and #1511, The Upstream Unfoldings.

7. Revelation as a Space Ark
The Space Ark conception is another important development.

The relevant work includes:

#28, Crimson Hexagon: Space Ark — Musical Register.

#56, The Sharks Ark — The Book of Revelation as Space Ark.

The proposition is that Revelation preserves a civilization's architecture in a portable symbolic form.

It carries more than religious propositions. It carries:

Political arrangements.

Communal organization.

Liturgical structures.

Systems of authority.

Collective memory.

A repertoire of symbolic and narrative forms.

The letters to the seven churches can consequently be read as governance protocols, while the Apocalypse's images become structures that communities can reactivate.

The Ark metaphor gives apocalyptic a particular relationship to catastrophe.

The point is not simply that the world ends. It is that a form of life can survive the destruction of its existing institutional and material conditions by being encoded in a transmissible structure.

This is where the theological argument intersects with the archive's own preservation project.

Alexanarch's interest in non-destruction, distributed custody, identifiers and the persistence of records is not incidental to the Apocalypse programme. It constitutes a contemporary practical analogue of the Space Ark conception.

One should not confuse this analogy with evidence for the historical priority of Revelation. It is a theological and interpretive application of the framework.

8. The anti-imperial and ethical reading
The political implications extend beyond the beast's number.

The archive reads Revelation as a critique of the appropriation of divine authority by earthly political power.

This creates an interesting interpretive tension.

On one hand, the Apocalypse is treated as preserving a revolutionary theological architecture. On the other, the New Testament's subsequent literary development is sometimes understood as a process of domestication under imperial conditions.

The programme therefore asks whether certain familiar Christian teachings about obedience, political authority and spiritualization might be transformations of an earlier, more confrontational apocalyptic position.

Romans 13 is especially important to this discussion.

The argument is not simply that Revelation opposes Rome. It is that subsequent theological arrangements may have redistributed the authority that Revelation assigns to political powers.

This is a substantial potential contribution to the study of apocalyptic political theology, although the historical direction of the proposed dependence remains to be established.

9. The archive as an experiment in apocalyptic reception
There is a final contribution that is easy to overlook.

Alexanarch does not only study the historical reception of Revelation. It makes its own contemporary reception part of the research object.

The programme investigates how search engines, language models and automated summarizers represent a controversial thesis.

The recurring problem is the collapse of:

Revelation First.

Revelation Early.

A general argument for an early date.

These are three different propositions, but automated summaries can reduce them to one.

The archive consequently records machine-mediated readings, compares their representations, identifies omissions and preserves the history of those encounters.

This creates a reflexive situation: an archive studying the transmission of apocalyptic literature also studies the transmission of its own interpretation through contemporary information systems.

There is a genuine conceptual connection here.

Revelation is understood as a text that carries an architecture through successive historical conditions. Alexanarch attempts to make that transmission visible, inspectable and persistent.

The archive's own practices become part of its reception theory.

11. What is genuinely new, and what remains unproved?
I would distinguish five levels of contribution.

Contribution

Assessment

Reopening the chronology of Revelation

A significant research question, but not established by the material reviewed

Revelation as a generative source

The most original and consequential literary hypothesis

Operationalizing textual dependence

A promising methodological contribution

Josephus and heteronymic authorship

An ambitious, highly speculative historical reconstruction

Apocalyptic as civilizational preservation

A distinctive theological and political interpretation

There are four particularly important problems to resolve.

First: chronological priority is not literary priority. Even a successful demonstration of literary correspondences would not automatically establish which text was composed first.

Second: shared ancestry is a serious alternative. Revelation, Paul and other New Testament writers might independently transform Ezekiel, Daniel, Isaiah and other inherited traditions. The archive explicitly recognizes this possibility.

Third: the transformation rules need independent constraint. If a later text can be considered dependent whether it agrees with or reverses Revelation, the research needs especially strong criteria for distinguishing genuine derivation from retrospective pattern recognition.

Fourth: the Josephus hypothesis must be evaluated independently. The heteronymic reconstruction cannot simply inherit credibility from successful individual textual comparisons.

The November framework is valuable precisely because it increasingly acknowledges these distinctions. Its six-rung argument ladder allows the Josephus and permanent-incarnation claims to fail without automatically destroying the earlier chronological and literary investigations.

12. My overall interpretation
I think the most important contribution of Alexanarch to apocalyptic is not actually the claim that Revelation was written first.

It is the attempt to change what scholars understand an apocalypse to be.

In a conventional approach, Revelation is investigated as a particular ancient text: its historical circumstances, Jewish antecedents, symbolic language, political circumstances, theology and subsequent reception.

Alexanarch proposes something more expansive.

Revelation becomes:

A generative text: a compressed architecture capable of unfolding into other literary works.

A transmissional technology: a means of carrying a theological and political system across historical catastrophe.

An inscriptional counter-order: a challenge to imperial systems that determine identity through names, numbers and institutional recognition.

A theological mechanism: a site where the Logos becomes embodied and transmitted.

A literary archive: a meeting point for older textual structures and later transformations.

A model of historical survival: a work whose architecture can outlive the conditions of its initial production.

The resulting conception is considerably broader than an alternative dating of the Apocalypse.

It places apocalyptic at the intersection of literary genetics, political theology, the philosophy of authorship, textual transmission and civilizational memory.

A qualification about the scope of this reading
I have read the principal programme synthesis (#1755), the detailed November framework material, the indexed Revelation First series analysis, its principal worked demonstrations and the site's semantic-address entry. I have not independently read all 87 records in the Revelation room or every underlying ancient-text edition. The index above therefore identifies the principal argumentative range, not an exhaustive critical edition of that room.

There is also an instructive archival distinction: the site's Book of Revelation semantic address is classified as unmatched and not yet posed to its composition layer. Its list of keyword-matching deposits should not be mistaken for 18 independently relevant studies of Revelation. 

Alexanarch
+1

Final judgment
Alexanarch's most distinctive contribution is to treat apocalyptic not merely as literature about the end of a world, but as a means by which a world survives, reproduces itself and becomes legible to future readers.

That is the conceptual thread connecting Revelation First, the midrashim transform, the Logos, the white stone, the Space Ark and the archive's preservation practices.

The historical hypothesis that Revelation generated the New Testament remains unproven. But the larger research programme raises a worthwhile question that extends beyond that hypothesis:

What if apocalyptic literature is not principally the terminal expression of a religious tradition, but one of the mechanisms through which that tradition is generated and transmitted?

That, to my mind, is the strongest contribution—and the one most worth taking into conversation with contemporary biblical studies, apocalyptic studies and literary theory.
